s0001: Justify how fossils (of the same land organisms) serve as evidence that the continents were once joined
s0002: Ask yourself whether the organism could cross the ocean on its own: if fossils of the same age from an organism that cannot fly and cannot swim in the sea are found on two continents, the continents were joined at that time.
s0003:
Mesosaurus was a reptile that lived about 280 million years ago and was about 1 meter long. Scientists think it lived in the shallow waters of lakes and coasts and could not swim across a wide, open ocean.
Its fossils have been found in rocks of the same age in South America and Africa, which are now separated by the Atlantic Ocean.
What conclusion can be drawn from this observation?
s0004: When Mesosaurus lived, these two continents were joined to each other.
s0005: Mesosaurs swam across the Atlantic Ocean and migrated to the other continent.
s0006: Mesosaurs appeared separately on the two continents, independently of each other.
s0007: Ocean waves carried Mesosaurus fossils from one continent to the other.
s0008: Mesosaurus: lived in shallow water, could not swim across the ocean
s0009: First, let's pick out the key information in the problem: this animal could not cross a wide ocean.
s0010: Fossils: South America + Africa, rocks of the same age
s0011: Even so, its fossils have been found on two continents that are separated by an ocean today.
s0012: Crossing the ocean ✗  ⇒  the continents were joined
s0013: If the animal could not cross the ocean, then at that time there was no ocean between the two continents; they were one connected landmass.
s0014: Answer: A) the continents were joined
s0015: So the correct conclusion is option A.
s0016: A student who chose B ignored the important information in the problem: it "could not swim across a wide, open ocean."
s0017: A student who chose C thought that the same species could appear separately in two places; a species appears in only one place and then spreads.
s0018: A student who chose D thought the fossils were moved later; in fact, on both continents they lie inside rocks of the same age, which means the animal lived in those places.
s0019: Think about how the animal could have gotten from one continent to the other.
s0020:
Malika, a scientist, is testing the idea that two continents now separated by an ocean were once a single landmass.
Which of the following observations supports this idea MOST STRONGLY?
s0021: Swallows of the same species build nests on both continents today.
s0022: Fish of the same species live in the waters near the coasts of both continents.
s0023: Fossils of the same land plant, whose heavy seeds are not carried far by wind or water, have been found in rocks of the same age on both continents.
s0024: Active volcanoes and earthquakes occur on both continents.
s0025: Condition for evidence: the organism must not be able to cross the ocean on its own
s0026: Only organisms that cannot cross an ocean can prove that the continents were joined.
s0027: A: birds fly ✗;  B: fish swim ✗
s0028: Swallows can fly and fish can swim from one continent to another, so they are not evidence.
s0029: D: volcanoes are found in many places ✗
s0030: Volcanoes and earthquakes also occur in many regions that were never joined to each other.
s0031: C: land plant with heavy seeds, fossils of the same age ✓
s0032: If fossils of a plant whose seeds cannot cross the ocean are found on both continents, then the continents were joined at that time.
s0034: The correct answer is option C.
s0035: A student who chose A did not consider that birds can fly across the ocean; besides, this is a present-day observation, not ancient evidence.
s0036: A student who chose B did not take into account that fish swim freely in ocean water and can move between continents.
s0037: A student who chose D thought volcanoes showed that the continents were similar, but volcanoes exist in many parts of the world and do not prove the continents were joined.
s0038: Find the organism that cannot cross the ocean by itself.
s0039: Apply the advantage of terrace (stepped) farming on mountain slopes in protecting soil from erosion
s0040: Remember that on sloping land, rainwater flows quickly and washes the soil away; terraces divide the slope into horizontal steps, slowing the flow of water and letting it soak into the soil.
s0041:
The picture shows an orchard laid out in terraces (steps) on a mountain slope in the Fergana Valley.
What is the MAIN advantage of this method?
s0044: The steps shade the plants from sunlight and protect them from scorching.
s0045: On the steps, plants can grow without any watering at all.
s0046: Rainwater flows slowly on the steps and soaks into the soil, so the soil is not washed away.
s0047: The steps always keep the soil fertile, even without fertilizer.
s0048: Sloping hillside: rainwater flows fast → soil is washed away (erosion)
s0049: On ordinary sloping land, rainwater runs downhill quickly and carries away the fertile topsoil.
s0051: A terrace divides the slope into flat steps, and each step holds back water.
s0052: Water flow slows down and soaks into the soil → less erosion
s0053: Because the water flows slowly, it soaks into the soil and the soil is not washed away.
s0054: So the main advantage is option C.
s0055: A student who chose A thought that terraces shade the plants; in fact, the steps do not block the light.
s0056: A student who chose B stretched the idea that "water is held back" too far; a terrace saves water, but it does not completely remove the need for watering.
s0057: A student who chose D confused protecting the soil with making the soil fertile; a terrace does not add minerals by itself.
s0058: Imagine what happens to the soil on sloping land after heavy rain.
s0059:
Jasur's grandfather planted almond trees on two mountain slopes with the same steepness. He left slope 1 as it was, and on slope 2 he built terraces (steps) (see the picture).
After heavy spring downpours, which statement about the two slopes is correct?
s0063: Less soil is washed off slope 1, because water runs off it quickly.
s0064: Less soil is washed off slope 2, because on the steps the water slows down and soaks into the soil.
s0065: The same amount of soil is washed off both, because they are equally steep.
s0066: More soil is washed off slope 2, because water collects on the steps.
s0067: Same steepness; the difference is the terraces
s0068: The two slopes differ in only one way: slope 2 has steps.
s0069: Slope 1: water flows fast → carries soil away
s0070: On a slope without terraces, water speeds up and washes away the topsoil.
s0071: Slope 2: water slows down on the steps → soaks into the soil
s0072: On the steps, water flows with stops and starts, much of it soaks into the soil, and the soil is not washed away.
s0074: So the correct answer is option B.
s0075: A student who chose A thought that fast-flowing water is helpful; in fact, fast-flowing water washes away more soil.
s0076: A student who chose C looked only at the overall steepness and did not consider that terraces slow down the flow of water.
s0077: A student who chose D thought that water collected on the steps washes the soil away; still water does not carry soil away, it soaks into it.
s0078: Compare where water flows faster and what fast-flowing water does to the soil.
s0079: Read a graph of how the pulse (breathing rate) changes after exercise and choose the conclusion that matches the data

s0081:
Malika's resting pulse is 75 beats per minute. She ran for 2 minutes, then measured her pulse every minute and drew a graph. The shaded part is the running time.
What conclusion can be drawn from the results?
s0086: Her pulse increased by 130 beats per minute.
s0087: After she stopped running, her pulse returned to its starting value in 4 minutes.
s0088: At minute 3, her pulse was 90 beats per minute.
s0089: Her pulse took less time to fall than it took to rise.
s0091: We read from the graph: at the start the pulse is 75, and at the end of the run it is 130 beats.
s0093: So the pulse increased by 55 beats, not by 130; this took 2 minutes.
s0095: The point at minute three is at 110, and 90 belongs to minute four.

s0098: So the correct conclusion is option B.

s0108: His breathing rate took more time to rise than it took to fall.
s0109: At minute 3, his breathing rate was 28 breaths per minute.
s0110: After the exercise ended, his breathing rate returned to its starting value in less than 5 minutes.
s0112: We read from the graph: 16 at the start and 34 breaths at the end of the exercise.
s0114: So the breathing rate increased by 18, and this took 1 minute.
s0116: Twenty-eight belongs to minute two, and at minute three it is 22 breaths.
s0117: Back to 16 at minute 5:  $5 - 1 = 4$ minutes $< 5$ minutes
s0118: At minute five it returned to 16, that is, 4 minutes after the exercise, which is less than 5 minutes.
s0120: So the correct conclusion is option D.
s0121: A student who chose A took the highest value (34) as the change; in fact, the increase is $34 - 16 = 18$.
s0122: A student who chose B compared the times the wrong way around: the rise lasted 1 minute, and the fall lasted 4 minutes.
s0123: A student who chose C read the point from one minute earlier: 28 is the value at minute 2.

s0125: Know that life on Earth first appeared in water in the form of single-celled organisms

s0128: Flowering plants that grow on land
s0131: Single-celled organisms that live in water
s0133: Life on Earth first appeared in water and moved onto land much later.
s0134: The very first: single-celled organisms (in water)
s0135: The oldest living organisms were simple single-celled organisms that lived in water.
s0137: Reptiles, mammals, and flowering plants appeared hundreds of millions of years after them.
s0138: So the correct answer is option D.

s0140: A student who chose B thought of reptiles as "ancient" animals, but for a long time before them there were only organisms that lived in water.

s0158: Apply the idea of competition between crops and weeds for water, minerals, and light to explain a situation

s0160:
Nilufar planted tomato seedlings in her garden plot. A few weeks later, weeds grew up among the seedlings.
Why is it important to pull out the weeds?
s0161: The weeds eat the tomato fruits.
s0162: The weeds compete with the tomatoes for water and minerals in the soil and for sunlight.
s0163: The weeds add too many minerals to the soil and poison the tomatoes.
s0164: The weeds take in all the air that the tomatoes need.
s0165: A plant needs: water, minerals, light
s0166: Every green plant needs water, minerals, and sunlight to grow.
s0168: Weeds also take up water and minerals from the same soil and block light with their leaves.
s0169: Limited resources → competition → tomatoes get less
s0170: Because resources are limited, there is competition between them, and less is left for the tomatoes.

s0172: A student who chose C thought weeds add minerals to the soil; in fact, they take minerals from the soil.

s0175:

s0177: The weeds ate the cotton bolls.

s0188: A student who chose B confused weeds with pest animals; plants do not eat other plants.

s0191: Know that even a single-celled organism carries out life processes such as excretion, respiration, and reproduction, in addition to feeding
s0192: Recall the life processes common to all living organisms, and use the organism's structure (does it have chloroplasts, lungs, roots?) to choose the process that fits it.

The picture shows a single-celled organism, the common amoeba. To live, the amoeba feeds: it takes in food and digests it.
Which other life process MUST the amoeba carry out to live?
s0199: Carrying out photosynthesis to make organic substances

s0202: Absorbing water from the soil through roots

s0230: A student who chose C transferred animal organs to a single-celled organism; a single cell has no heart.

Marmots and wolves live in a mountain pasture. The wolves have no natural enemies in this pasture.
From 1940 to 2000, scientists counted both animals every year and showed the results on a graph. Wolves hunt marmots.
How are the changes in the numbers of the two animals related?
s0270: After the number of marmots increases, the number of wolves also increases a little later, because they have more food; after the wolves increase, the number of marmots decreases.

s0273: The numbers of the two animals change randomly, independently of each other.

s0277: When there are many marmots, the wolves have enough food and their numbers grow.
s0278: Many predators → prey decrease → then predators decrease too

s0303: Use a chemical formula to find the number of atoms of each element in a molecule

s0410: She brings rod 1 close to rod 2: if they attract each other, rod 2 is a magnet.
s0411: She brings end X of rod 1 close to ends P and Q of rod 2, one at a time: if either end is repelled, rod 2 is a magnet.
s0412: She brings end X of rod 1 close to ends P and Q of rod 2: if both ends are attracted, rod 2 is a magnet.
s0413: She weighs both rods on a scale: if their masses are equal, rod 2 is a magnet.
